bodies.intuition: Hide one distinctive sentence in a very long document and ask the model to find it. It is the standard long-context demonstration, it produces a satisfying green grid, and it is much easier than almost anything a reader actually wants to do with a long context.
bodies.engineer: The reason it is easy is that the needle is lexically distinctive and the task is single-hop retrieval — one lookup, no aggregation, no comparison, no reasoning over anything found. Models that saturate it fail on tasks that require tracking several facts across the same context, or noticing that a fact is absent. So a perfect score is evidence about retrieval and no evidence about use, and the two get reported as though they were the same claim.
bodies.math: Difficulty scales with the number of items that must be held at once, not with the length of the context. A single needle is one item however long the haystack; multi-hop questions over the same document require holding several and relating them, and accuracy falls with that count far faster than with length. So a benchmark that varies only length is varying the axis that matters least, which is why saturating it says less than it appears to.

viz.caption: Contexts where the model finds what it was asked for, against ones where it does not, by how distinctive the target is. Drag the distinctiveness up to a single odd sentence and watch the task become trivial — which is where this benchmark sits, and why saturating it proves little.
